warmup.q: Two consumers wait on an empty queue with if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); return queue.removeFirst();. A producer adds one item and calls notifyAll(). What happens?
options: One consumer gets the item and the other keeps waiting
Both wake; one gets the item and the other throws NoSuchElementException
notifyAll() wakes only one of them, so nothing goes wrong
warmup.why: notifyAll() wakes both. They get the lock back one at a time. The first takes the item. The second is already past its if, so it calls removeFirst() on an empty queue. With while instead of if, the second would check again and go back to waiting.

sections.h: A guarded block waits for a condition without burning a core
sections.html:
A consumer thread has nothing to do until a payment arrives. The worst way to wait is to spin:

Java
while (!ready) { }     // checks the flag as fast as the core can go
Kotlin
while (!ready) { }     // the same spin in Kotlin

The demo below measured it. To wait one second, the spinning thread used about 1,026 ms of CPU: a whole core, doing nothing useful. The thread that waited properly used 0 ms. (The spinner's flag also has to be volatile, or the JIT may read it once and loop forever. The memory model track explains why.)

The proper way is a guarded block. You hold the lock, check the condition, and call wait() if it doesn't hold yet:

Java
synchronized (lock) {
    while (!ready) {
        lock.wait();      // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take the lock again
    }
    // here ready is true, and we hold the lock
}
Kotlin
synchronized(lock) {   // lock is a java.lang.Object here: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
    while (!ready) {
        lock.wait()       // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take the lock again
    }
    // here ready is true, and we hold the lock
}

wait() does three things in order. It releases the monitor, so other threads can get in and change the state. It parks the thread in the monitor's wait set, in the WAITING state, using no CPU. And when the thread is woken, it takes the monitor back before wait() returns.

The thread that changes the state calls notifyAll(), holding the same lock:

Java
synchronized (lock) {
    ready = true;
    lock.notifyAll();     // wake every thread waiting on lock
}
Kotlin
synchronized(lock) {
    ready = true
    lock.notifyAll()      // wake every thread waiting on lock
}

notifyAll() does not hand over the lock. The woken threads move to the monitor's entry set, the threads waiting to get in, where they show as BLOCKED and compete for the lock like any newcomer. None of them can run until the notifier leaves its block.

You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait() or notifyAll() on. Call them outside synchronized (lock) and you get IllegalMonitorStateException at once. That rule protects you. The condition can only change while someone holds the lock, so a waiter can't check the flag, miss the change that happens next, and then wait forever.

try.title: Spin vs wait
steps: Run BusyWaitDemo. Both threads wait one second for the same event. Predict the CPU time of each.
In the waiter, delete the synchronized line around the while loop and its closing brace, so lock.wait() runs without the lock. Run it again.

code.title: BusyWaitDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. */ public class BusyWaitDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); static boolean ready; // guarded by lock static volatile boolean readyForSpinner; // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs volatile public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinner = new Thread(() -> { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can }, "spinner"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait(); // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } } } }, "waiter"); spinner.start(); waiter.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // the authorization takes a second to come back ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000; // measure while both still wait long waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000; readyForSpinner = true; synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join(); waiter.join(); System.out.printf("spinner used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", spinCpu); System.out.printf("waiter used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", waitCpu); } }

alt.title: BusyWaitDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() private var ready = false // guarded by lock @Volatile private var readyForSpinner = false // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs @Volatile fun main() { val spinner = thread(name = "spinner") { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can } val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait() // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() return@thread } } } } Thread.sleep(1_000) // the authorization takes a second to come back val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000 // measure while both still wait val waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000 readyForSpinner = true synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join() waiter.join() println("spinner used about $spinCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") println("waiter used about $waitCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") }

try.expect: The spinner uses about a full second of CPU to wait one second. The waiter uses close to zero. Without the synchronized block, the waiter dies at once with IllegalMonitorStateException: you can only wait on a monitor you hold.

sections.h: Always wait in a while loop, never an if
sections.html:
When wait() returns, the condition you waited for may not hold. There are two reasons.

The first is in the Javadoc for Object.wait: "A thread can wake up without being notified, interrupted, or timing out, a so-called spurious wakeup." It is rare. It is also allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting if it is not met.

The second reason happens all the time. notifyAll() wakes every waiter, but they take the lock back one at a time, and other threads may get in first. Two consumers wait on an empty queue. A producer adds one item and calls notifyAll(). Consumer 1 gets the lock first and takes the item. Consumer 2 gets the lock next, and the queue is empty again. If consumer 2 checked with if, it is already past its check:

Java
if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait();   // checked once, before waiting
return queue.removeFirst();         // NoSuchElementException
Kotlin
if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait()    // checked once, before waiting
return queue.removeFirst()          // NoSuchElementException

With while, consumer 2 checks again, sees the empty queue and goes back to waiting. That is all a guarded block is: a while loop around wait(), with the condition as the loop test.

The habit costs nothing, so make it unconditional. Every wait() sits inside while (!condition). In a code review, treat an if around wait() as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It has just never had two waiters at the same time yet.

try.title: Steal a wake-up
steps: Read IfInsteadOfWhile. Both consumers are parked before main adds one item and calls notifyAll().
Run it and read both consumers' lines.
Change if (queue.isEmpty()) to while (queue.isEmpty()). Predict what each consumer prints, then run it again.

code.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. */ public class IfInsteadOfWhile { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); static String take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait(); } return queue.removeFirst(); // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable consumer = () -> { try { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " took " + take()); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " failed: " + e); } }; Thread c1 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-1"); Thread c2 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-2"); c1.start(); c2.start(); while (c1.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10); // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1"); // one item... lock.notifyAll(); // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000); c2.join(2_000); if (c1.isAlive() || c2.isAlive()) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting System.out.println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item"); synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2"); lock.notifyAll(); } } c1.join(); c2.join(); } }

alt.title: IfInsteadOfWhile.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque // Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val queue = ArrayDeque<String>() private fun take(): String { synchronized(lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait() } return queue.removeFirst() // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } fun main() { val consumer = Runnable { try { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} took ${take()}") } catch (e: Exception) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} failed: $e") } } val c1 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-1") val c2 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-2") c1.start() c2.start() while (c1.state != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.state != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10) // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1") // one item... lock.notifyAll() // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000) c2.join(2_000) if (c1.isAlive || c2.isAlive) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item") synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2") lock.notifyAll() } } c1.join() c2.join() }

try.expect: With if: one consumer takes auth-1, the other fails with java.util.NoSuchElementException. With while: one takes auth-1, the other re-checks, waits again, and takes auth-2 when main gives it a second item. Which consumer wins can change from run to run.

sections.h: Prefer notifyAll, because notify wakes one thread, maybe the wrong one
sections.html:
notify() wakes one thread from the wait set, and you don't get to choose which. That is fine when every waiter waits for the same condition and any one of them can use the change. It breaks when one monitor has waiters for different conditions.

A bounded buffer is the classic case. Producers wait for "not full", consumers wait for "not empty", and with a plain monitor they share one wait set. Picture a buffer with one slot, two producers and two consumers, all using notify():

  1. The slot is empty, so both consumers wait.
  2. Producer 1 fills the slot and wakes consumer 1. Before consumer 1 gets the lock, both producers find the slot full and wait. The wait set now holds producer 1, producer 2 and consumer 2.
  3. Consumer 1 empties the slot and calls notify(), which happens to wake consumer 2, the wrong kind.
  4. Consumer 2 finds the slot empty and waits again. Consumer 1 loops, finds it empty too, and waits.

Now all four threads wait for a signal nobody will send. No thread holds the lock, so it isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense, but the program has stopped just the same. The demo below gets there within a handful of items.

So the default is notifyAll(). It wakes every waiter, each one re-checks its own condition in its while loop, and the ones that can't go on wait again. The price is extra wake-ups when many threads wait, which rarely matters next to a stalled pipeline.

Use notify() only when both of these hold: every waiter waits for the same condition, and one change lets at most one of them proceed. If you need precise wake-ups for two kinds of waiters, give each kind its own Condition on a ReentrantLock. That is lesson 7 of this track.

try.title: Stall a pipeline with notify()
steps: Run NotifyStall. Two producers and two consumers share a one-slot buffer that signals with notify().
Read the thread states it prints when progress stops.
Run it again with -Pargs=all, which switches both signals to notifyAll().

code.title: NotifyStall.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A one-slot buffer shared by 2 producers and 2 consumers. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. */ public class NotifyStall { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<Integer> slot = new ArrayDeque<>(); static final AtomicLong moved = new AtomicLong(); static boolean all; // set once in main, before the threads start static void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); slot.addLast(x); signal(); // notify() wakes ONE waiter: maybe a consumer, maybe the other producer } } static int take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); int x = slot.removeFirst(); signal(); return x; } } static void signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll(); else lock.notify(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); System.out.println(all ? "using notifyAll()" : "using notify()"); Thread[] threads = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { boolean producer = i < 2; threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1); else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, (producer ? "producer-" : "consumer-") + (i % 2)); threads[i].setDaemon(true); threads[i].start(); } long last = -1; for (int second = 1; second <= 5; second++) { Thread.sleep(1_000); long now = moved.get(); if (now == last) { System.out.printf("stalled after %,d items. Thread states:%n", now); for (Thread t : threads) System.out.println(" " + t.getName() + ": " + t.getState()); return; } System.out.printf("after %d s: %,d items moved%n", second, now); last = now; } System.out.println(all ? "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiter, so the right kind always gets a turn" : "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again"); } }

alt.title: NotifyStall.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong // A one-slot buffer shared by 2 producers and 2 consumers. Uses notify(), or notifyAll() with -Pargs=all. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val slot = ArrayDeque<Int>() private val moved = AtomicLong() private var all = false // set once in main, before the threads start private fun put(x: Int) { synchronized(lock) { while (!slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() slot.addLast(x) signal() // notify() wakes ONE waiter: maybe a consumer, maybe the other producer } } private fun take(): Int { synchronized(lock) { while (slot.isEmpty()) lock.wait() val x = slot.removeFirst() signal() return x } } private fun signal() { if (all) lock.notifyAll() else lock.notify() } fun main(args: Array<String>) { all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" println(if (all) "using notifyAll()" else "using notify()") val threads = List(4) { i -> val producer = i < 2 Thread({ try { while (true) { if (producer) put(1) else { take(); moved.incrementAndGet() } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } }, (if (producer) "producer-" else "consumer-") + (i % 2)).apply { isDaemon = true start() } } var last = -1L for (second in 1..5) { Thread.sleep(1_000) val now = moved.get() if (now == last) { println("stalled after %,d items. Thread states:".format(now)) threads.forEach { println(" ${it.name}: ${it.state}") } return } println("after %d s: %,d items moved".format(second, now)) last = now } println(if (all) "no stall: notifyAll() wakes every waiter, so the right kind always gets a turn" else "no stall this time; it depends on timing, so run it again") }

try.expect: With notify() it stalls almost at once (runs here stopped after 2 or 3 items) with all four threads WAITING. With notifyAll() it moves tens of thousands of items a second for the full five seconds.

sections.html:
Put the three rules together and you get the bounded buffer you'll write in the lab. A bounded buffer sits between producers and consumers. It holds at most capacity items, so a fast producer has to wait for slow consumers instead of filling the heap. That waiting is called backpressure.

Java
public class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;

    public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.size() == capacity) {   // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait();
            }
            items.addLast(item);                 // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll();                    // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    public T take() throws InterruptedException {
        synchronized (lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait();
            }
            T head = items.removeFirst();
            lock.notifyAll();
            return head;
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) {
    @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN")
    private val lock = Object()                    // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait()
    private val items = ArrayDeque<T>()

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)           // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version
    fun put(item: T) {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.size == capacity) {       // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up
                lock.wait()
            }
            items.addLast(item)                    // 2. act: condition holds, lock held
            lock.notifyAll()                       // 3. signal: the state changed
        }
    }

    @Throws(InterruptedException::class)
    fun take(): T {
        synchronized(lock) {
            while (items.isEmpty()) {
                lock.wait()
            }
            val head = items.removeFirst()
            lock.notifyAll()
            return head
        }
    }
}

Each method has the same three parts. The guard is a while loop that waits until the method can proceed. The act changes the state, safely, because the condition holds and the lock is held. The signal wakes the other side, because the state they wait on just changed.

A few choices in there are deliberate.

The lock is a private object, not this. Any code that can reach an object can call wait() or notify() on it. With a private lock, only the buffer can signal its own waiters.

Both methods signal with notifyAll(), because producers and consumers share one wait set, as the previous section showed.

Both methods declare throws InterruptedException. wait() throws it when the waiting thread is interrupted, and the buffer can't know what the caller wants to do about that, so it lets the caller decide. That is the second option from lesson 2 of this track: propagate.

In production you won't write this class. ArrayBlockingQueue does the same job, faster and with timeouts, and lesson 9 of this track covers it. You write it once so that put and take stop being magic, and so that a thread dump full of threads waiting inside a queue makes sense to you.

Check your model before the lab. Delete the notifyAll() in take(). Two producers fill a buffer of capacity 2 and then wait in put(). A consumer takes one item. What happens next? (The producers stay in wait(): the take made room, but nothing woke them. The consumers drain the buffer and then wait too, until every thread is waiting.)

figure.caption: wait() moves the owner to the wait set and gives the lock back. notify moves a waiter back to the entry set, where it must win the lock again, so it must re-check its condition.

analogy: A monitor is a meeting room with one key. People who want the room queue in the corridor (the entry set, BLOCKED). The one inside can decide they can't continue yet, hang the key back up and go to the lounge next door (the wait set, WAITING). When someone in the room changes things, they can call into the lounge: notify() sends one person back to the corridor, notifyAll() sends everyone. Nobody walks from the lounge straight into the room. They queue for the key again, and by the time they get in, the thing they waited for may be gone, which is why they must look again. The analogy breaks at spurious wakeups: people don't leave the lounge for no reason, but a Java thread is allowed to.
world: You'll rarely hand-write wait() in a payments service, and when you do it should look like the buffer above. You meet guarded blocks all the time inside libraries. A connection pool with 20 connections makes the 21st request wait until a connection is returned. A KafkaProducer blocks send() for up to max.block.ms when its buffer memory is full. A Quarkus worker pool queues requests when every worker is busy. In a thread dump those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Reading the stack tells you which condition they wait for, and that usually tells you which resource ran out.
mistake: The most common real mistake is using wait() and notify() as a bare signal, with no condition to check: one thread calls lock.wait() "until the result is ready", another calls lock.notify() when it is. If the notify happens before the waiter starts waiting, the signal is lost and the waiter sleeps forever. This is a lost wake-up. It passes tests because the waiter usually gets there first. The fix is to always wait for a state, never for an event: set a field such as ready = true under the lock before notifying, and wait with while (!ready) lock.wait();. A notify that came early is then harmless, because the waiter sees ready and never waits.

compare.title: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: BoundedBuffer.java
java.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

kotlin.title: KotlinGuarded.kt
kotlin.html: package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Kotlin's Any has no wait()/notify(). The idiomatic guarded block uses a Lock and a Condition. class KotlinBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() // one wait set, like a monitor's private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) changed.await() // same while-loop guard items.addLast(item) changed.signalAll() // same as notifyAll() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) changed.await() items.removeFirst().also { changed.signalAll() } } } fun main() { val buffer = KotlinBuffer<Int>(2) val consumer = thread { repeat(5) { println("took ${buffer.take()}") } } repeat(5) { buffer.put(it) } consumer.join() }

compare.note: Kotlin's Any does not expose wait(), notify() or notifyAll(). The Kotlin samples in this lesson get them by using a java.lang.Object as the lock, which works but earns a compiler warning that you have to suppress. The idiomatic replacement is a ReentrantLock with a Condition: withLock { } takes and releases the lock, await() plays the part of wait(), and signalAll() the part of notifyAll(). The rules don't change. Condition allows spurious wakeups too, so you still wait in a while loop. As a bonus, one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers can wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds on exactly that.

worked.title: Wait for a settlement file, with a deadline

steps.say: A batch job must wait until the settlement file has arrived, but give up after 30 seconds. Here is the first attempt. What can go wrong?
steps.code: boolean awaitFile() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000); return fileArrived; } }

alt.html: fun awaitFile(): Boolean { synchronized(lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000) return fileArrived } }

steps.say: It is the if bug in a new shape. A spurious wakeup, or a notifyAll() meant for some other condition on the same lock, returns early with fileArrived still false, after 2 seconds instead of 30. Simply putting wait(30_000) in a while loop is wrong too: every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The fix is to compute a deadline once and wait for what is left of it.
The guard loop now checks the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the remaining time.
steps.code: boolean awaitFile(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos(); // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized (lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition long leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000; if (leftMillis <= 0) return false; // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis); // 4. wait only for what's left } return true; } }

alt.html: fun awaitFile(timeout: Duration): Boolean { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos() // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized(lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition val leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000 if (leftMillis <= 0) return false // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis) // 4. wait only for what's left } return true } }

steps.say: The side that receives the file sets the state before it signals, both under the lock. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter sees fileArrived and never calls wait(). Why does the waiter use System.nanoTime() and not System.currentTimeMillis()?
steps.code: void onFileArrived() { synchronized (lock) { fileArrived = true; // state first lock.notifyAll(); // then the signal } }

alt.html: fun onFileArrived() { synchronized(lock) { fileArrived = true // state first lock.notifyAll() // then the signal } }

steps.say: nanoTime() only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is wall-clock time, and NTP can move it backwards or forwards, which would stretch or cut the timeout.

lab.title: Build a bounded buffer with wait and notifyAll
steps: Run the tests. All six fail, some only after a few seconds, because the threads that should wait die instead.
Add the fields: a private lock object, an ArrayDeque for the items, the capacity. Reject a capacity below 1 in the constructor.
Write put: guard with while (full) lock.wait();, add at the tail, notifyAll().
Write take: guard with while (empty) lock.wait();, remove the head, notifyAll(), return it. Write size() under the lock.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more. The 4-producer, 4-consumer test is the one that catches if and notify() mistakes.
hints: The blocking tests poll getState() until it says WAITING. A thread that sleeps in a loop shows TIMED_WAITING and fails them. Use wait() with no timeout.
Call wait() and notifyAll() on the same object you synchronize on. Calling wait() on this while holding lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException.
Don't catch InterruptedException inside the buffer. Let it propagate: both methods already declare it.
lab.done: All six tests in BoundedBufferTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A bounded buffer from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. In a blank file, write a bounded buffer of String with put and take, using synchronized, wait and notifyAll. Then check: is every wait() inside a while? Do both methods signal? Did you use a private lock?

answer.html: public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() @Throws(InterruptedException::class) // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version fun put(item: T) { synchronized(lock) { while (items.size == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait() } items.addLast(item) // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll() // 3. signal: the state changed } } @Throws(InterruptedException::class) fun take(): T { synchronized(lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() } val head = items.removeFirst() lock.notifyAll() return head } } }

recap: A guarded block holds the lock, checks a condition, and calls wait() until it holds. wait() releases the monitor while it waits and retakes it before returning.
You must hold an object's monitor to call its wait(), notify() or notifyAll(), or you get IllegalMonitorStateException.
Always while (!condition) wait();. Spurious wakeups are allowed, and another thread may change the state before you get the lock back.
notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter. With two kinds of waiters on one monitor it can wake the wrong kind and stall everything. Default to notifyAll().
Wait for a state, not an event: set a field before notifying, so an early signal is never lost.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a bounded buffer built on one monitor needs while loops and notifyAll(), and what goes wrong if you use if or notify() instead.
explain.answer: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty", but with one monitor they share one wait set. When a thread wakes, the state may already have changed again, because other woken threads can get the lock first, and spurious wakeups are allowed. So each waiter must re-check its condition in a while loop; with if, a consumer can wake up and remove from an empty buffer. notify() wakes one arbitrary waiter, which may be the wrong kind: a consumer waking another consumer wastes the only signal, and eventually every thread waits with nobody to wake them. notifyAll() wakes everyone, and the loops send the ones that can't proceed back to waiting.

deeper.html:
Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. wait(millis) returns when notified, interrupted, spuriously, or when the time is up, and it does not tell you which. That is why the worked example tracks its own deadline with System.nanoTime().

The JVM has bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That is a good reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write.

Two observability notes. JFR has a jdk.JavaMonitorWait event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a jdk.JavaMonitorNotify event. And on virtual threads, Object.wait() used to pin the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases.

Finally, the history. wait/notify have been in Java since 1.0. java.util.concurrent arrived in Java 5 with Condition, BlockingQueue and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. When you read the source of ArrayBlockingQueue, you'll find the same guard, act and signal parts as in this lesson, written with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions.
